blocks.text: **The problem.** Design a **Least Recently Used (LRU) cache** with a fixed `capacity`. `get(key)` returns the value if the key is cached, otherwise -1. `put(key, value)` adds or updates a key; if that makes the cache hold more than `capacity` keys, it **evicts the key used least recently**. Both operations must run in **O(1)** average time. Using a key — `get` or `put` — makes it the most recently used.

blocks.alt: An LRU cache with capacity 3 holding keys 3, 1 and 2, in order of use. On the left, a hash map from each key to its node. On the right, a doubly linked list between two sentinel nodes, head and tail: the most recently used entry, 3, sits right after head, and the least recently used, 2, right before tail. Getting key 1 moves its node to the front; putting a new key when the cache is full evicts the node before tail.

blocks.text: The idea: a hash map for finding, a doubly linked list for ordering

The cache needs two things at once. It must **find** a key's entry in O(1) — that's a hash map. And it must keep entries **in order of use**, so that it can move any entry to the front and remove the oldest from the back, also in O(1) — that's a **doubly linked list**. An array can't move an item from the middle to the front without shifting; a singly linked list can't unlink a node without first finding the node before it. A doubly linked node knows both neighbours, so moving or removing it is a few pointer changes.

The map stores **key → node**, so `get` jumps straight to the node, unlinks it and re-adds it at the front. Two **sentinel** nodes, `head` and `tail`, sit at the ends permanently: the list is never truly empty, so unlinking and adding never need a null check. The least recently used entry is always `tail.prev`.
1. Brute force: an array of keys in order of use
**Time O(capacity) per operation, space O(capacity).** Finding the key in the order array and shifting the array after removing it are both linear. Correct, but not the O(1) the question asks for.

blocks.caption: The map finds the node; the list moves it to the front or drops the one before tail.

blocks.code:
class Entry:
    def __init__(self, key, value):
        self.key = key
        self.value = value
        self.prev = None
        self.next = None


class LRUCache:
    def __init__(self, capacity):
        self.capacity = capacity
        self.map = {}                      # key -> its node, so any entry is found in O(1)
        self.head = Entry(0, 0)            # sentinels: head.next is the most recently used,
        self.tail = Entry(0, 0)            # tail.prev the least recently used
        self.head.next = self.tail
        self.tail.prev = self.head

    def _remove(self, node):               # unlink a node in O(1)
        node.prev.next = node.next
        node.next.prev = node.prev

    def _add_front(self, node):            # insert right after the head sentinel
        node.prev = self.head
        node.next = self.head.next
        self.head.next.prev = node
        self.head.next = node

    def get(self, key):
        node = self.map.get(key)
        if node is None:
            return -1
        self._remove(node)                 # it was just used: move it to the front
        self._add_front(node)
        return node.value

    def put(self, key, value):
        if key in self.map:
            self._remove(self.map[key])
        node = Entry(key, value)
        self.map[key] = node
        self._add_front(node)
        if len(self.map) > self.capacity:
            lru = self.tail.prev           # the least recently used is at the back
            self._remove(lru)
            del self.map[lru.key]

blocks.text: **Time O(1) per operation, space O(capacity).** Each operation is a hash lookup plus a constant number of pointer changes. The node stores its **key** as well as its value so that, when it's evicted from the back of the list, the map entry can be deleted too.

Most languages ship this combination: JavaScript's `Map` remembers insertion order (delete and re-set a key to refresh it), Python has `collections.OrderedDict` with `move_to_end`, and Java's `LinkedHashMap` takes an access-order flag and a `removeEldestEntry` hook. Each is a hash map threaded through a doubly linked list — the interview wants you to build it yourself.

rows.timeWhy: One **hash lookup** plus a constant number of **pointer changes**.
rows.spaceWhy: One map entry and one node **per cached key**.

blocks.text: LRU Cache is one of the most asked design questions of all, because it combines two data structures so that each covers the other's weakness.

items: **Capacity 1** — every new key evicts the previous one.
**Putting an existing key** — update its value and make it the most recent; the size doesn't change and nothing is evicted.
**Get refreshes recency** — after `get(1)`, key 1 must not be the next evicted.
**Evict, then get** — the evicted key returns -1, and the map must not still hold it.
**Forgetting the key in the node** — then eviction can't find which map entry to delete.
**LFU Cache** (Hard) — evict the least **frequently** used: a doubly linked list per frequency, plus a map to each node.
**Design Browser History** — a doubly linked list without the map. Earlier in this chapter.
**All O(1) Data Structure** (Hard) — increment, decrement and min / max key in O(1): buckets in a doubly linked list.
